newsitem.title: USA: Michigan income gains top list in U.S. in 2nd qtr.
newsitem.headline: Michigan income gains top list in U.S. in 2nd qtr.

text.p: Residents of Michigan saw their incomes surge this past spring, while earnings gains of those in Wyoming lagged the rest of the nation, according to the latest Commerce Department statistics.

Americans' wallets generally grew fatter this past spring as pay raises were seen in a variety of industries. U.S. personal income rose 1.7 percent in the second quarter after rising by 1.2 percent in the first.

The income gain for the April-June quarter was the largest jump since the first quarter of 1995 and was more than double the 0.8 percent increase in prices paid by U.S. consumers, suggesting rising living standards.
In Michigan, earnings climbed 3.0 percent, but edged up just 0.5 percent in Wyoming. Wyoming was the only state where earnings grew more slowly than prices in the second quarter.
In addition to Michigan, seven other states enjoyed income growth that was more than a half-percentage point above the U.S. average.

Those were Idaho and North Carolina, both with earnings growth of 2.6 percent, Nebraska and Utah, with increases of 2.5 percent, South Dakota with a rise of 2.4 percent and Arkansas and Kentucky, both with 2.3 percent.

"In most of the fastest growing states, increases in earnings were above average in both durable goods and non-durable goods, manufacturing, in finance, insurance and real estate, and in construction," the department said.
It said above-average income growth in durable goods manufacturing in Michigan reflected a rebound from the effects of the General Motors Corp strike in the first quarter.
"Earnings also increased at above-average rates in services in Idaho, Nebraska and Utah, in wholesale and retail trade in Utah, and in retail trade in Kentucky," it said.
Maine, Hawaii, Rhode Island, Montana and New York joined Wyoming in having income growth that lagged the national average by a half-percentage point or more.
Income was up 0.9 percent in Maine, 1.0 percent in Hawaii and Rhode Island, and 1.2 percent in Montana and New York.
Commerce said that in the slower-growth states, earnings either rose at below-average rates, were unchanged or declined in transportation and public utilities and government.
New York saw a decline in earnings in transportation and public utilities that reflected a step-down in bonus payments from a high level in the first quarter.
Construction earnings fell in Hawaii, Maine and Wyoming.
